content.thinking:
I'm planning out a hunched Warcraft-style swamp troll, roughly 2.6-2.7 meters tall, and setting up the coordinate conventions and joint hierarchy before building the skeleton carefully to avoid runtime issues.

I'm placing the hips, spine chain, neck, and oversized hunched head with tusks and a jaw joint, then working out shoulder and arm positions for the long Warcraft-style limbs.

For the arms, I'm checking that upper-arm and forearm lengths (0.62 and 0.7) span the distance from shoulder to hand, bending the elbow backward with a hint direction, and naming the shoulder/elbow/wrist chain so the path ends at the wrist tip joint.

For hands, I'm keeping it simple: a chunky palm shape with separate finger chains attached to the wrist, each finger a short two-joint chain (three fingers plus a thumb per hand), parented to the wrist tip, with claw spikes capping the ends.

Now I'm positioning the arm hanging down, palm box extending below the wrist, fingers pointing downward and slightly forward with some spread, thumb tucked to the inside. For the legs, I'm placing the hip joint and foot target, checking that the limb segment lengths can reach that distance with a forward bend.

Lower leg chain: hip, knee, ankle with the ankle as the tip bone. I'm keeping toes as rigid parts rather than separate joints, just attached capsule shapes on the ankle bone, then feeding the resulting joint path into the chain function.

For torso skinning, I'm using a loft across spine stations bound to the spine chain and hips joint, bending the skin along the path. Since both hips and the first spine joint sit at roughly the same parameter t≈0, I'm ordering the bone list carefully so the later entry wins the weighting at that point, though this feels a bit fragile.

To make it more robust, I'm matching the torso loft's path exactly to the spine chain's catmull curve, defining consistent control points so both the skeleton and the skin geometry trace the same spine shape.

I'm expanding the spine control points to add more stations for pelvis, belly, chest, and shoulders, giving the torso a hunched, big-bellied troll silhouette with varying width and height at each station.

Defining spine points...

Still defining neck and head joints...

Now I'm planning the spine chain to start at the hips position, and the leg chains to parent explicitly off the hips joint at their offset positions. For the head, I'm setting up the skull and facial parts using world coordinates offset from the head joint location.

Since parts are placed with explicit bone references anyway, I'll just use world coordinates everywhere and skip local-space complications.

Now I'm sketching the troll head design: long face, flat broad nose, heavy brow, deep-set glowing yellow eyes, jutting jaw with upward tusks, swept-back pointed ears, and a mohawk crest of spikes running down the neck. For the swamp troll aesthetic I'm thinking mottled green-teal skin with mossy patches, warts, a lighter belly, and bone/tooth fetish necklaces, trinket bundles on the belt, and hide loincloth details.

I'm settling on a palette: swamp-green mottled skin shading toward dark teal and yellow-green moss tones, a vivid crimson-orange mohawk, glowing yellow eyes, ivory tusks and bones, and brown hide garments. For the skin I'm layering nested countershading and mottling paints to get a hand-painted, warm-top/dark-underside gradient look rather than a toon shader, and I'm considering adding ambient occlusion-style shading on top for extra depth.

Verifying the smoothstep clamping works correctly, then estimating texel density based on painted surface area—roughly 30 square meters would need to support the target resolution.

I'm settling on a 2048 paint sheet with a 4096 atlas, since that's heavier but needed for crisp detail across many painted parts, following the rule of halving when things don't fit. I should keep mesh geometry reasonably simple to avoid issues with painting fine details, and I'm thinking the mohawk could use card-based geometry with SVG feather/spike textures running from brow to nape and down the neck and upper back.

Since I'm unsure whether the distribute/along API actually returns frame arrays or just takes a callback, I'll build the frames manually using the frame function with a point and direction instead of relying on uncertain return values. For the mohawk cards, I'm working out the orientation math -- frame up-axis, flow direction pointing back, and computing the side vector as the cross product of up and back to get the card's width direction.

Actually I realize I want the mohawk sheets facing sideways rather than facing backward, so flow should point along x instead, which puts the card's width along z -- that's the sagittal-plane orientation I need for spikes running down the center of the head and spine. I'm deciding to switch approach entirely: instead of cards, I'll build the mohawk from extruded blade shapes (~9-10 of them) along the head and neck, chunky and low-poly like a Warcraft style, each with a tapered outline and a red-to-orange gradient paint.

Defining the swept-back blade outline...

Now I'm thinking about bone attachments for the mohawk blades — using head bone for upper pieces, neck and spine bones for the lower ones, with explicit `bone:` and `at` placements, then mapping out positions along the skull from brow to back using the head joint coordinates.

I'm sketching the troll's head geometry: a flattened cranium sphere positioned and scaled for a sloping forehead, angled brow ridge rods for a heavy look, and now working out the muzzle/face shape using a scaled sphere or frustum form.

I'm placing a wide flat nose with dark nostril spheres, cheekbone spheres, and dark eye socket ellipsoids under the brow holding small glowing yellow eye spheres with black pupils.

Still shaping jaw geometry...

Still writing tusk geometry...

Realizing the snout is too narrow there, I shift the tusk base outward to sit just outside the snout's widest point near the cheek, curving the tusk points up and slightly back with a defined radius taper.

Now I'm placing small secondary teeth: spikes on the lower jaw and a few cones under the upper lip, plus a dark reddish box to suggest the mouth's interior shadow between jaw and snout.

For the ears, I'm shaping a swept-back pointed leaf outline, positioning it high and to the side so it extends backward and outward like a dragon's ear.

I'm also adding a tiny gold torus hoop earring near the ear base for detail, then starting the mohawk/hair strip, laying out blade points that trace from the forehead across the top of the cranium down toward the nape and upper spine.

Still working out blade placement...

I'm tracing the back surface contour along the spine to plot where the mohawk ridge should sit, mapping y-z coordinates from the nape down through the trapezius hump to the lower back.

Still working out the surface-raycasting logic...

I'll fall back to the spine's first joint when no bone hit is found, using the hit's position directly. Now I'm working out blade orientation so the +x and +y axes stay roughly perpendicular, adjusting the lean-back direction so the outline doesn't skew.

Checking the outline polygon for self-intersections...

Now I'm thinking through the mohawk blade design: scaling each blade's outline by height, arranging roughly 14 across the head and back with taller ones at mid, and applying a dark crimson-to-orange-to-yellow color gradient.

Shifting to the torso, I'm setting up a loft sweep between hips and spine bones to build the body shape.

For skin coloring, I'm working out a belly patch effect using smoothstep functions based on surface normal and vertical position to blend a lighter tone onto the belly region, while making sure it doesn't accidentally bleed onto the arms.

I'm now considering adding tribal war paint stripes as a decorative element—maybe applying white or yellow stripes on the face, chest, and arms, possibly using an SVG decal projected onto the torso near the chest.

Adding tribal sigil decals to chest and shoulders plus face decals, then setting up the arm rig: shoulder joint position, a tapered sweep chain for each arm with smooth radius values, and a scaled sphere for the deltoid at the shoulder.

Now I'm computing the shoulder-to-hand distance to figure out arm bend, positioning the elbow joint to flex backward slightly so the long troll arms reach down near the knees, with hands ending around the knee height. I'm also starting to block out the palm geometry as a flattened box shape.

Writing finger chain sweeps...

Now I'm tallying up the joint count: four digits per hand with two joints each gives sixteen finger joints total, plus spine, neck, head, jaw, arms, and legs bringing the rough total near forty. I'm deciding toes should be rigid sweeps attached directly to the ankle bone rather than separate chains, and ears stay rigid on the head too, skipping extras like a tail or hanging accessories for simplicity.

Now I'm working out leg placement: hip positions, foot targets, and shaping the foot as a capsule sweep running from heel to ball with slightly different radii so the sole sits flat against the floor at the right height.

The shin sweeps down to the ankle fine, with the radius tapering from 0.11 there. For the leg chain I'm sizing a smooth taper of thigh-knee-ankle radii, roughly 0.21 down to 0.11, plus a knee cap sphere, and setting the bend hint so the knee points forward.

Checking the limb helper function — it takes root, target, lengths, and a bend direction, returning the chain of joint points. I verify the leg segment lengths work out geometrically for a natural bend, then reconsider pelvis proportions since the wide-set, thick thighs stick out past the current pelvis width, so I'm widening the pelvis to better match. Now I'm thinking about how to add a loincloth or fur skirt around the hips, considering a lathe-based shape for it.

For that I need to pin down actual spine coordinates and widths at each station, so I'm laying out approximate x/y/z positions, widths, and heights for the pelvis, belly, chest, and upper torso, then checking how the front-facing silhouette at each height compares to where the head sits, since the head seems to be projecting further forward than the chest does.

For the loincloth, I'm thinking through how to generate a closed belt loop around the pelvis -- either tracing an ellipse manually around the pelvis center or using a surface loop helper anchored to a point on the torso with a lift offset to keep it sitting properly on the hip geometry.

Shaping the loincloth flap outline...

I'm estimating the belly's front radius at that height to be around 0.28, so the flap would hang vertically from about z=0.3 down toward the thighs, where it needs to clear the forward curve of the knee.

I'm also working out the tilt direction for the flap so it flares outward and swings down-forward correctly, adjusting the y-direction vector to get the right angle.

For the leather texture, I'm defining a paint function that mixes brown tones with noise for a mottled grain, plus dark spots and a red war-stripe band across the material.

Now I'm shifting to the bone fetish necklace -- planning a sweep along a closed loop around the neck/collar area to represent a cord with hanging teeth and skull pieces draping over the chest.

I'm sketching coordinates for the collar loop points around the neck, then reconsidering the trapezius hump shape—trying a scaled sphere positioned to slope up into the neck without making it too tall like a mohawk.

For the necklace itself, rather than computing exact surface intersections (risky given the body's unknown geometry), I'll just drape it: snap each rough path point to the nearest surface among the torso, hump, and neck meshes with a small lift offset, accepting that any cord segment that ends up inside the body will simply be hidden visually.

Then to hang teeth and skull pendants, I'll sample the draped path manually at evenly spaced parameters, filter for points on the front-facing half of the body, and place downward-pointing bone spikes there plus a few larger skull pendants (sphere plus jaw box with dark eye sockets) centered at the front.

For the belt fetish bundle, I'm building a helper that ties together bone shapes, feather extrudes, beads, and a small skull on a cord hanging from a red cord, positioned at the left and right hips using ray casts against the torso surface to find accurate anchor points.

I need to check that these hanging items clear the thigh's outer radius, which is larger than the pelvis half-width, so I'm nudging the hang position slightly outward and angling it toward the front so the bundle drapes past the thigh rather than clipping into it.

For the shoulder armor I'll give the left side a horned skull pauldron with bone spikes and feathers, and the right side bone-plate tusk armor instead. Then I'm adding wrist bracers with hide wraps and bone beads, plus forearm cuffs as closed rings positioned along the arm chain.

Still writing cuff geometry...

I'll add a wrist wrap with closed red leather strip circles at a couple points, elbow bone spikes jutting backward, and consider small knee or shoulder spikes for the troll silhouette, skipping a dorsal ridge in favor of mohawk handles, plus hanging feather cards later.

For feathers, I'll place card geometry facing upward with a 180-degree lean so they drape downward near the fetish and mohawk, using two tinted feather textures (red and teal) with a center rib, kept sparse without any glow. For swamp flavor, I'm considering moss tufts, hanging vines, and small mushroom caps scattered across the shoulders and head using draped card textures.

Now I'm scattering green fringe cards across the hump, shoulders, and head top using a normal-based filter, plus hanging moss strands from the shoulders, and adding a mud-brown gradient paint on the lower legs blended with noise. I'm also planning tiny mushrooms on the hump built from stem cylinders and cap spheres, along with small lighter-colored wart spheres scattered across the face, back, torso hump, and arms using embedded sphere geometry at scatter points.

Skipping navel and nipples, but adding scar decals on the chest as part of the war paint. For the eyes, I'm building a glowing yellow sphere with a flattened black pupil, topped with a skin-colored eyelid dome scaled and positioned to overlap the upper half, aiming for an angry brow shape where the inner brow point sits lower than the outer point, aligned with the eye position relative to the cranium's front curvature.

Now I'm working through the full head geometry step by step: placing the cranium sphere with specific radii, positioning the brow as an angled rod that protrudes past the cranium surface, and calculating eye socket positions by checking where they sit relative to the cranium's curved surface to make sure they're embedded just under the brow ridge.

Adding the nose bridge as a capsule shape with a tip sphere and small flared nostril spheres, plus dark nostril indents.

Now I'm sketching the upper lip as a curved sweep from the snout corners up to the center using a catmull path, considering a darker lip color against the jaw tone.

Next I'm placing small downward teeth spikes beneath the lip line, then building the lower jaw as a swept U-shaped mass from the jaw joint outward, plus a fill sphere under the chin to round out the shape.

I realize the jaw's top surface would sit higher than the upper lip's bottom edge, which works fine for a closed mouth with overlapping teeth. For a slight snarl, I'll pose the jaw bone with a small forward-tilting rotation to open the mouth a bit, but only after building all the jaw geometry so the pose doesn't affect part placement.

I'm settling on about a 10° rotation at the jaw hinge, giving roughly a 0.07 gap — enough for a believable opening. I'll apply that jaw pose at the very end of the head build so all parts land in their correct built positions first, then get carried by the pose transform afterward.

Now I'm placing the tusk bases just inside the jaw, with each tusk following a curved bezier path rising alongside the muzzle and outward near the cheek spheres.

Skipping the chin spike idea, I move to the ears, positioning them on the head angled outward, backward, and upward, and working out an orthogonal direction vector so the ear's cross-section plane sits correctly relative to its extrusion axis.

Now I'm defining the ear's shape—a long pointed outline about 0.5 in length and 0.08 wide—and setting up its coloring so most of the ear uses the skin tone but a thin inner band gets a pinkish shade to suggest the inner ear, using a conditional based on position. Next I'll add gold hoop earrings as torus shapes.

Working out torus positions...

I'll place small gold stud spheres along the lower edge of the ear instead, positioning them so they poke slightly through the thin ear surface for a pierced-earring look. For the neck, I'm considering a tapered sweep shape going from wider to narrower.

Checking continuity: the neck needs to match the torso radius at its base and the cranium radius at its top, with a rounded cap so it tucks neatly inside the skull geometry. I'm also sketching in a small scaled sphere for a shoulder/hump bulge near the base of the neck.

The hump bulges past the torso's back edge, giving a hunchback silhouette, and sits low enough under the head to read as heavy trapezius muscle. Shoulder spheres flare out well beyond the torso's half-width, making the troll read as broad and massive, putting overall body width around 1.9 units.

Now I'm designing a skull helper that builds a cranium, jaw, eye sockets, nose hole, and teeth from a handful of primitives, planning to reuse it for five hanging skulls at roughly seven parts each. I'm setting up a bone-colored paint shader that mixes tan tones for subtle shading across the surface.

I'm defining a general "shaded" gradient helper that mixes dark and light colors based on surface normal, planning to apply it broadly across skin, hide, bone, and metal materials for that painted Blizzard look, while keeping an eye on the total flat-color count to stay within limits.

Now I'm fleshing out the fetish/necklace details—a draped loop with pendants, including a skull pendant with glowing green eyes using the glow kit, going for that eerie voodoo aesthetic. I'm also planning glowing yellow eyes for the main character using a similar emissive technique.

For body detail, I'm sketching out a tribal chest sigil as an SVG decal—spiral-eyed mask motifs, claw-slash stripes, and a sun-circle rendered in ochre-white and red tones, sizing the stroke widths so they stay crisp at raster resolution. Then I'm positioning this decal on the torso using surface coordinates and direction vectors so it wraps naturally across the chest.

Next I'm placing shoulder tattoo decals near the shoulder sphere surfaces with mirrored positions for left and right, then adding small war-paint stripe decals on the cheeks under each eye, working out their surface coordinates and outward-facing directions so they sit correctly on the face geometry.

I'm weighing whether the small cheek spheres are large enough for decal projection to succeed reliably, and considering using a tiny flat plane geometry instead as a simpler, safer alternative to a decal for face details, while reserving actual decal projection for larger surfaces like the torso where it's safer and more reliable.

The sag leaves a small gap but it's acceptable at this scale, so smaller planes around .08×.06 should work fine; maybe simpler to just paint the stripes directly as part of the skin texture instead of separate geometry.

I'm defining diagonal war-paint bars within a cheek zone using modular stripes based on position—checking the bounds so the pattern stays confined to the face and doesn't bleed into the eye region above y=2.36.

I'll also add a chest tattoo as a separate decal for richer detail, keeping the paint technique for the head/face region. For moss, I'm designing tuft and strand SVG textures—one for scattered clumps on the hump and shoulders, another for hanging draped strands with a tapered leaf shape and wavy vertical form.

Now I'm attaching those moss cards to the shoulder surfaces, binding them explicitly to the shoulder joint bone so they stay rigid with the model. For mushrooms on the hump, I'm building a stem-and-cap part using a tapered cylinder for the stem and a half-sphere for the cap, painted red with a cream stem, and considering adding spot details via paint.

On the right shoulder I'm planning a bone-plate pauldron instead: a lathe-generated hide dome shape tilted outward from the shoulder top, which will serve as the base for mounting curved bone spikes and a hide strap.

Working out spike placement around the dome axis...

I'm aiming for roughly 350-450 parts total, using Vector3 math for bone offsets rather than over-engineering it. I still need to add belts, bracers, and bone fetish details like necklaces, pauldron skulls, bone arm bands, and hair-tied bone beads.

For the gold tusk caps, I'm positioning torus rings around the tusks using a tangent-aligned sweep, scaling the ring radius to match the tusk's taper at that point along its length.

Now I'm sketching the loincloth, belt, and hanging fetish items as cord sweeps, and tightening the flat colour palette down to a handful of entries like dark ink for pupils and nostrils, a deep mouth tone, and golds and yellows for the eyes and metalwork, keeping the total count well under the limit.

Writing imports and type declarations...

Now I'm setting up the builder with the swamp troll's name and texture size, then defining the skeleton starting with the hips joint and spine chain coordinates.

Building the spine chain and torso loft...

That dome extension pushes the pelvis bottom down to y=0.73, which hangs awkwardly between the legs like a diaper bulge. I should switch to a flat cap at y=1.2 instead, cutting the pelvis flush at hip level so it doesn't dip below where the thighs begin.

Shifting the pelvis start to y=1.12 with a round cap, I'm checking the dome radius (0.475) against the thigh width — it extends down to about y=0.7, tapering between the legs, but the loincloth should cover that region anyway so it's probably fine. I'm considering simplifying further with a pointed cone cap instead.

Actually, I'll narrow the first loft station so the cap is smaller, adjusting positions and widths for the pelvis and hip-thigh attachment points to keep proportions consistent. Then I'm setting up a neck chain using a catmull curve through three points, parented to the spine's last joint, with two named segments matching the two curve spans.

Now I'm defining the head and jaw joints parented to the neck, using group tagging for head-related parts, and setting up the cranium as a non-uniformly scaled sphere mesh attached to the head bone with a skin color applied.

I'm writing a reusable blob helper function that creates sphere parts with configurable position, scale, color, and segment detail, pulling in the proper paint and fill types for coloring.

Now I'm sketching out a skull-building function that assembles a cranium sphere and a muzzle box with proportional scaling based on a skull-width parameter, positioning the muzzle below and in front of the cranium.

I'm adding the jaw block, dark eye socket spheres with an optional glow for green eyes, a small nose cavity, and a row of tooth boxes along the muzzle's front bottom edge.

Still writing merge helper...

Continuing the fetish bundle, I'll add the red cord, crossed bone pieces with knobbed ends, a hanging skull, feather cards, and alternating colored beads along the cord. For the bone shape, I'm building a capsule shaft with knob spheres at each end offset by a perpendicular vector to suggest the joint ends.

Now I'm building the arm chains symmetrically for left and right sides, defining shoulder-to-wrist limb points and attaching them as a chain parented to the spine, working out which spine joint index the shoulder should connect to.

That matches the doc example with a bare direction array for two segments, so that's fine. For the arm sweep, I'm defining a radius function tapering along the chain with a skin color, with the elbow positioned early along the path parameter.

Now I'm positioning the hand: a palm sphere near the wrist joint, with knuckle row and finger base points offset across the hand width, keeping palms facing inward toward the thighs with fingers pointing down and thumbs forward, matching a natural hanging-arm pose.

Setting claw segment dimensions and radii, then naming each finger joint in the chain and sweeping skin-colored geometry along it to form the digits.

Now I'm defining the thumb's three-joint path with coordinates offset from the wrist, tapering radii from base to tip, and considering where to attach forearm cuffs along the arm chain using its positional and normal data.

For the cuff I'm sweeping a closed path with an elliptical cross-section rather than a round one, using the normal/binormal frame to give it a broad flat band shape, but I need to work out whether those frame vectors stay in-plane or axial for a planar circular loop under parallel transport.

I'll go with a simple rope-like tube for the wrist wraps and sphere beads on the cuff, plus a bone-colored torus-ish armband with studs around the bicep, keeping part counts modest. Now I'm setting up the leg chains by computing hip and foot joint positions per side and generating limb points for a hip-knee-ankle chain.

I'm defining the leg's radius profile with a thigh-to-ankle taper and a slight calf bulge, then shaping the foot as a capsule from heel to toe that properly overlaps the ankle joint, and placing three toe bases spaced along the foot's width.

Now I'm sizing the toe tips and claws so they sit just above the floor without clipping, assigning bone weights for the foot parts to the ankle joint, and starting to add a small knee spike detail projecting outward from the knee joint.

Adding knee spikes, then an ankle anklet made from a closed ring with hanging tooth-like spikes, and skipping fur detail for the hips and thighs. Now I'm setting up surface attachment points on the torso, hump, neck, and cranium so the mohawk blades can be placed correctly on each body part.

I'm casting downward rays at various z-positions along the back to find where each blade should sit, then scaling blade heights so they're tallest near the head and taper off toward the tail, checking the first hits against the cranium's front profile.

Blade orientation uses a basis leaning back for the sloped surface. I'm noticing the mohawk blade thickness and spacing values would cause heavy overlap between adjacent blades given their width relative to spacing, so I need to adjust those dimensions.

I'll narrow each blade's width so they overlap only partially, creating a dense spiky crest rather than a solid wall. For coloring, I'm deciding to use a single shared gradient paint across all mohawk blades based on height, mixing colors by vertical position in meters so shorter blades naturally show less of the tip color than taller ones, giving variety without needing a separate paint per blade.

I'm defining the mohawk gradient as a piecewise mix through dark crimson, bright red, orange, and pale gold moving up the blade height. I'm skipping extra details like braid beads and hand hair, but adding a small gold nose ring positioned at the septum as a nice accent, then moving on to texture work for moss tufts.

Writing SVG moss blade shapes...

Adding lighter chevron barbs and a teal feather variant, then working out how to hang feathers from cards using frame orientation and lean rotation so the tip points downward correctly.

For moss, I'm scattering points on the hump surface and generating standing tufts via cards with lean, bend, and spin variation, using cross:true for visibility from multiple angles. Now I'm thinking about hanging moss from the shoulder, considering explicit frame positions along the top rim of the shoulder spheres.

For shoulder moss, I'll filter scatter points by upward normal, build frames per hit tied to the shoulder joint bone, and use drooping cards sized small to medium, about six per shoulder. I'm skipping vines but adding warts as small embedded spheres scattered across the torso and cranium, colored a lighter green to contrast with the base skin tone.

For the chest decal, I'm raycasting the torso's front surface to find a hit point, using that hit's normal to orient the decal's direction while defaulting to world-up, and sizing it to cover a good portion of the chest. I'm handling the case where the raycast might fail with a fallback before placing the decal texture over the base color.

Now I'm thinking through the eyes using a glowing sphere part, then working out the belt as a looped sweep around the torso at a fixed height, considering whether to make it a thin rope-like tube or a wider flattened band, and wrestling with how to orient the tube's cross-section correctly along the loop.

I'm also planning to add decorative studs—small gold spheres placed at intervals around the belt path using position sampling along the curve.

For the buckle, I'll scan the loop for the point facing most toward the camera and anchor a skull ornament there, offset slightly outward. Then I'm working out how to attach front and back hide flaps hanging from the belly, making sure the orientation vectors stay orthogonal so they drape naturally rather than tilting.

I'm now checking for clearance between the flap and the thighs/knees -- estimating the knee's forward z-position by interpolating between hip and foot, and it looks like the knee pokes out further forward (around z=.49) than the flap's position (z=.38), so the flap should clear the legs without intersecting them.

With front clearance settled, I'm sketching the back flap by casting a ray backward from the belt area to find where it attaches, then moving on to pauldron placement and considering using a lathe-based dome shape for that piece.

Positioning the lathe dome at the shoulder joint, tilting its axis outward so it caps the shoulder sphere properly, and estimating where the base and top radii should land relative to the shoulder center.

For the rim studs, I'll need a helper that computes a basis of perpendicular vectors around the dome's axis, then scatters small gold spheres evenly around that ring. I'm planning asymmetric dome decorations too -- a skull and curved horns on the left shoulder, five bone spikes on the right -- plus a bone ornament for the head.

Now I'm thinking through a back totem piece and a diagonal bandolier strap draped across the chest with bone beads and a hip pouch, built by sweeping a curved path from shoulder to hip and giving it a bead-like radius profile along its length.

Actually, that strap would collide with the chest tattoo decal, so I decide to drop it and keep the chest simpler with just the tattoo and necklace instead. I'm also planning the necklace with pendants, a possible second choker, skipping a tail since trolls don't have one, adding bicep armbands with bone beads, skipping knuckle spikes, and considering hide leg wraps.

Now I'm setting up type definitions and color constants for the build—ink, mouth, gold, eye glow, cord, leather, skin tones—along with a shading helper that blends dark and light tones for the paint system.

Writing paint functions...

Still blending surface colors...

Still tuning color blend logic...

Writing flap paint logic...

Still shaping triangle pattern logic... Now I'm defining colors for the claw, mohawk, and gold paint details using the shading helper.

I'll set up a vector helper for building 3D points, then start writing a skull construction function that takes a position, scale, bone joint, eye color, and yaw rotation.

Writing skull body shapes...

Still writing teeth geometry...

For the skull I'm counting parts: cranium, muzzle, jaw, two eyes, nose, and teeth gives seven total, with faceted low-poly boxes and spheres kept chunky and blocky for the bone shading style.

Writing the bone helper function...

Still writing fetish geometry...

Still working out the necklace loop geometry, positioning points around the neck base where it meets the torso, draping down the chest and wrapping around the sides at varying radii.

Still writing drape and sweep logic...

For the pendants, I'm sampling the necklace path at regular intervals and filtering for points on the front/lower portion to place spike teeth, then picking the three lowest points for larger skull ornaments.

Now I'm adding head details: the cranium sphere with skin tone, positioned and scaled for the skull shape, and brow ridges built from capsule rods using the skin color on the head bone.

I'm skipping the forehead scar and secondary brow ridge, then working out teeth placement—upper teeth as small spikes curving along the jaw line using a parametric z-offset, attached to the head bone. Lower jaw I'm sweeping as a catmull curve for the U-shaped bone path with its own color.

I'm rigging the jaw sweep to the jaw bone with constant radius and rounded caps, filling in cheek volume with a scaled sphere, and adding a dark interior mouth box between the jaw halves. I consider adding a flattened pink tongue sphere but decide to skip it, then move on to thinking about a chin beard/tuft.

Deciding to skip the goatee, jaw studs, and nose warts for simplicity, I focus on the eyes -- adding upper eyelid spheres positioned to cover half the eye for an angry expression, with rotation left as optional.

I'm weighing whether to add a back totem pole with a skull and feathers for extra silhouette interest, but conclude the existing bone fetishes -- necklace, belt bundles, pauldron skulls, wrist bones, and mohawk beads -- already satisfy the brief well enough, leaving the totem as a budget-permitting extra.

I'll lower the totem so its height roughly matches the mohawk. For the skull orientation, I decide to let it face backward relative to the viewer and add a flip parameter that inverts z-offsets so facing can be reversed for both the skull and its teeth, keeping boxes symmetric.

Now I'm estimating part counts across all pieces -- body, hands, feet, mohawk, head, necklace, belt, pauldrons, totem, warts, mushrooms, cuffs -- landing around 400 total, which should keep triangle count manageable. I want the skull eye holes to glow with a pale green color, and I'm double-checking that the rod-drawing helper's color overload handles vector endpoints correctly before writing out the full code.

Next I'm extruding the ears using mirrored vectors for left and right sides, checking that the orientation axes stay roughly orthogonal, and defining the ear outline as a small polyline with a sharp point partway along its length to give it a tapered shape.

So the ear's normal points mostly outward in x, which confirms the ears flap sideways like elf ears rather than lying flat. I'm placing small gold stud spheres along the lower ear edge at a few interpolation points, then moving on to extruding the blade outline shape.

I'm defining the blade's polygon shape with five scaled points forming the base, sides, and sharp tip, and checking that the edges don't self-intersect by tracing through each segment's coordinates.
